Introduction Climate change has recently emerged as a paramount global concern, commanding significant attention from the business community and its diverse stakeholders (Trinh, 2024). The potential hazards associated with climate change—including global warming, rising sea levels, and an increased frequency of severe natural disasters such as hurricanes, droughts, and heavy rainfall—pose substantial threats (Stern, 2008; Burke, 2018; Hossain & Masum, 2022). Although climate risk is non-financial in nature, it is intrinsically linked to corporate financial performance. It is associated with poorer financial outcomes and the retention of more long-term debt, particularly in developing countries (Zhang et al., 2023; Chalabi-Jabado & Ziane, 2024; Bauri et al., 2025), where losses from natural disasters can lead to significant earnings and cash flow volatility (Huang et al., 2017). Consequently, climate risks have profound implications for corporate valuation and investment decisions (Krueger et al., 2020; South et al., 2021), drawing focused attention from both businesses and governmental organizations. A global climate survey conducted by the United Nations Development Program (UNDP) and the University of Oxford revealed that 64% of participants worldwide, and within Arab states, consider climate change a global emergency (Flynn et al., 2021). In response, various economic and regulatory instruments have been deployed to reduce carbon emissions; by 2020, carbon taxes covered over 20% of global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions (IPCC, 2023). Accordingly, companies worldwide are increasingly motivated to address climate change and enhance the transparency of their related disclosures (Abdesslem et al., 2025). Climate risk and its disclosures can directly affect the information presented in financial reports. Prior studies (Ding et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2024; Abdesslem et al., 2025; Le et al., 2025) have investigated climate change risk as a catalyst for earnings management, where firms may employ real or accrual-based techniques to maintain compliance with climate policies or smooth reported earnings to mask performance fluctuations (Le et al., 2025). * Corresponding author E-mail address s.abdelazim@mu.edu.sa (S. This assessment influences the evaluation of inherent risk, control risk, and the extent of audit procedures required to reduce detection risk and overall audit risk to an acceptable level (Stanley, 2011; Troug, 2020). Auditors perceive clients with elevated climate risks as having higher business risk due to increased earnings volatility and a greater propensity for earnings management, which can obscure poor results (Truong et al., 2020). This perception often leads to higher audit fees to compensate for incremental reputational and litigation risks (Stanley, 2011; Truong et al., 2020; Nguyen et al., 2023). Therefore, auditors increasingly factor clients' climate risks into their determination of the necessary audit effort (Yang et al., 2023). Despite this, a lack of specific guidance on auditing environmental matters persists within existing professional standards (Meleschenko et al., 2020). Recognizing this gap, auditing standard setters have begun to act. The International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board (IAASB), for instance, has issued a staff audit practice alert affirming the auditor's responsibility to consider climate change risks in the audit of historical financial statements (Hoque & Irfan, 2025). As independent gatekeepers to the securities markets, auditors are well-positioned to assess ESG risks, leveraging their expertise to identify potential material misstatements in financial statements. This interaction between ESG risks and the audit process influences both the required audit effort and fees. Investors appear to value this diligence, as firm value increases when environmental initiatives are considered in audit fee determinations (Sharma et al., 2018). Furthermore, politically connected firms, which often face high agency costs due to weaker oversight, have an incentive to enhance their legitimacy. They may do so by improving disclosure transparency and appointing more certified auditors (Liu et al., 2017; Najaf & Najaf, 2021), consequently paying higher audit fees due to their perceived risk (Gul, 2006). However, a review of the literature reveals a significant research gap regarding the moderating effects of ESG performance and political connections on the relationship between environmental disclosures and audit efforts. Given the growing emphasis on climate change, particularly in developing countries like Egypt, this study contributes to the accounting and auditing literature in several ways. First, it highlights climate change risk as a critical determinant of audit efforts, underscoring its role as a key business risk in the auditor's risk assessment. Second, while prior literature has primarily focused on client characteristics, this study addresses the scarcity of research on external factors like climate risk and its management. Finally, it provides novel evidence on the association between climate change risk and audit efforts, illustrating how environmental factors influence operational costs, including audit fees. The study also elucidates the moderating roles of corporate social responsibility, environmental strategy, and political connections in this relationship. The present study complements the existing environmental disclosure literature by: 1) enhancing the understanding of how voluntary climate disclosures impact the audit profession in Egypt, a developing country with recent environmental initiatives; 2) examining the effect of comprehensive ESG practices on the disclosure-audit effort dynamic; and 3) investigating the influence of political connections on this same relationship. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section 2 presents the contextual background. Section 3 reviews the relevant literature and develops the hypotheses. Section 4 describes the research design and methodology. Sections 5 and 6 present the main results and robustness tests, respectively. Finally, Section 7 discusses the empirical results and presents conclusions. 2. A contextual background The Egyptian government and financial institutions have launched several initiatives to support climate change disclosures, highlighting both the associated risks and opportunities. A pivotal step was taken on 5 July 2021, when the Egyptian Financial Regulatory Authority (FRA) issued Decrees No. 107 and 108. Effective for annual reporting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2022, these decrees mandate that listed companies on the Egyptian Exchange (EGX) with an issued capital or net equity greater than or equal to EGP 500 million must include climate-related financial disclosures in their annual reports. These disclosures must illustrate the financial implications of climate-related risks and opportunities (FRA, 2021). In response, major Egyptian banks began implementing these practices ahead of the deadline. For the year ended 30 June 2021, both the Commercial International Bank (CIB) Egypt and the National Bank of Egypt (NBE) published ecological footprint reports. These reports detailed their environmental impact across five key areas: carbon, water, plastic, waste, and land, alongside descriptions of their climate mitigation actions (CIB Ecological Footprint Report, 2021; NBE Ecological Footprint Report, 2021). Egypt further demonstrated its commitment by hosting the 27th United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP27) in Sharm El-Sheikh on 6 November 2022. The conference assembled nearly 35,000 representatives from 198 governments to strengthen climate action, with a key goal of reducing CO2 emissions by 45% by 2030 (compared to 2010 levels) to meet the Paris Agreement's target of limiting global warming to 1.5°C (UNDP, 2023). During COP27, and in response to recommendations from COP26, major Egyptian banks announced sustainable funding initiatives to finance investments in sustainability improvements. A. Literature review and research hypothesis 3.1 Climate change disclosures and financial statement Climate risks are classified into two main categories. First, physical climate risks which consist of physical risk event-driven (acute physical risk) which arises from weather related risks (i.e. Storms, flood, drought heat waves) and Chronic physical risk arises from long term shifts in climatic patterns including temperature changes which could lead to sea level rise. Second, transition climate risks which are related to efforts of developing a lower-carbon economy (i.e. policy, legal, technological, market and reputational risks). These risks could increase operating costs or asset impairment due to new or amended climate- related regulations. The entity's financial performance could also be affected by changing consumer demands and the development of a new technology (IFRS foundation, 2023). Firms can gain benefits from disclosing climate change-related information. Disclosing more information on climate change improves financial performance (Maji & Kalita , 2022). Climate change and sustainability reporting is still mainly a voluntary practice (Hahn et al., 2015) allowing management to choose the most relevant way for disclosing climate change related information, accordingly the level of information asymmetry between management and stakeholders is becoming higher. There are several theories interpreting and justifying managerial behavior of disclosing environmental and climate change information that are identified as agency theory, signaling theory, Institutional theory, and socio-political theories. First, agency theory assumes information asymmetry among managers and shareholders limiting their oversight and ability to detect opportunistic managers’ behaviors (Giannarakis et al., 2018). Environmental practices and voluntary environmental disclosures help to enhance information transparency, reduce information asymmetry, improve stockholders` oversight, and reduce agency costs associated with political and legislative actions can be reduced. (Radhouane et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2022). Second, signaling theory assumes the company which makes efforts to reduce climate change risks are more willing to voluntarily disclose climate change related information to signal positively and make a good impression on the market. (Guo et al., 2022; Talkhan& Ibrahim, 2024), thereby increasing firms’ potential market value (Matisoff et al., 2013). Third, institutional theory assumes institutional pressures and social interactions affect organizational actions. Hence, organizations with similar institutional pressures will eventually adopt similar strategies to gain legitimacy. (Herold, 2018; Wukich et al., 2024). Fourth, Socio-political theories, including stakeholder theory and legitimacy theory (Patten, 2002), assume social disclosure is a function of social and political pressures facing the company. Stakeholder theory explains the role of stakeholders in shaping management strategies. (Cotter & Najah, 2012) accordingly it considers stakeholders` power as a determinant of environmental disclosures. (Azuma & Higashida, 2024). Consequently, management has a moral obligation and a social contract with each group of stakeholders, not only shareholders. (Holder-Webb et al., 2008; Cotter & Najah, 2012; Datt et al., 2022). Legitimacy theory, probably the most widely used theory to explain the role of environmental disclosures, considers overall society and its role in organizational legitimacy and it assumes organizations exist to the extent that society considers them legitimate. (Radhouane et al., 2020; Talkhan& Ibrahim, 2024), accordingly firms with threatened legitimacy are likely to use voluntary disclosures to satisfy society`s expectations and establish legitimacy. (Clarkson et al., 2008; Guo et al., 2022). Regarding the existing International Standards on Auditing (ISAs) the majority are applicable to climate change risk and the related disclosures. Consequently, the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board (IAASB) has issued a Staff Audit Practice Alert to help auditors understand how the existing ISAs are related to climate-related risks in an audit of financial statements. According to ISA 3002 and ISA 3153 “Identifying and Assessing the Risks of Material Misstatement” auditors while assessing risk of material misstatements they should make inquiries about climate risk (i.e. Climate- related commitments, Management process of assessing climate risk). ISA 3204 requires auditors of clients affected by climate risk to consider these risks while determining materiality level, including related qualitative disclosures, management assessment of climate risks, and how climate risks have affected other judgments in relation to the recognition or measurement of financial statements items. According to ISA 3305 when climate-related risks form part of the assessed risk of material misstatement at assertion level, the auditor shall perform further procedures to get persuasive audit evidence. According to ISA 5706 climate-related risks could be related to event or condition that may considered as a significant doubt on the entity’s ability to continue as a going concern and the appropriateness of management’s going concern assumption (i.e. Extreme weather events are higher than before and may create significant litigation claims which may impact the entity’s ability to continue its operations). (IAASB, 2020). ISA 7017 requires an auditor to report key audit matters related to an account or disclosure that is material to the financial statements including subjective matters involving complex auditor judgement (such as estimates that incorporate climate-related risks). ISA 7208 obliged auditors to identify material inconsistency between financial statements and other Information included in the client`s annual report, including climate related disclosures, which may decrease the credibility of the financial statements and may even indicate potential material misstatements. (IAASB, 2020; Jeyaretnam et al., 2023). Climate risk, as a client`s systematic business risk, is one of the main factors that probably affect audit efforts and audit risk. Generally, a high level of business risk increases the level of audit risk which leads to raise audit efforts. Prior studies (Bell et al., 2001; Lyon & Maher, 2005; Kim & Fukukawa, 2013) empirically investigated the impact of auditors perceived business risk including climate change risk on the number of audit hours and audit fees. The results support that auditors are considering the client`s business risk while determining audit efforts and cost (Bell et al., 2001). Lyon & Maher (2005) found that audit clients of large audit firms with high perceived business risks in developing countries are associated with high audit fees, where the auditor can transfer his expected cost through higher audit fees. Consequently, many firms now integrate green management practices and objectives into their core strategies (Perez-Valls et al., 2015). This trend highlights a clear interaction between climate change risk and ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) performance. Prior literature has extensively investigated this interaction (Hummel & Schlick, 2016; Giannarakis et al., 2017; Braam & Peeters, 2018; Hossain & Masum, 2022; Chen et al., 2024; Duan et al., 2025). Hummel & Schlick (2016) note that the empirical evidence on the relationship between sustainability performance and disclosure is mixed, suggesting that voluntary disclosure theory and legitimacy theory are not mutually exclusive. Consistent with voluntary disclosure theory, superior sustainability performers are associated with high-quality disclosures to signal their performance to the market. Conversely, and in line with legitimacy theory, poor performers often decrease disclosure quality to conceal their true performance and protect their legitimacy. Supporting the voluntary disclosure perspective, Giannarakis et al. (2017) found a positive impact of ESG performance on climate change disclosure. Similarly, Braam & Peeters (2018) indicate that companies with superior sustainability performance are more likely to enhance their reports by obtaining third-party assurance, a relationship that is stronger in more shareholder-oriented countries. Hossain & Masum (2022) further found that corporate social responsibility is more effective in reducing climate change risk for firms with greater ESG disclosures. On the other hand, recent studies support the impact of climate risk on ESG performance. Chen et al. (2024), using a sample of Chinese firms, identified a negative relationship between the level of climate risk and ESG performance, an effect that is stronger for state-owned enterprises and firms with more institutional investors. In contrast, Duan et al. (2025) found that climate risk disclosure itself significantly improves corporate ESG performance, particularly on environmental metrics. Previous literature has also revealed implications of ESG activities for the audit process and the required level of audit effort. LópezPuertas‐Lamy et al. (2017) found that strong ESG performance minimizes the auditor's assessment of material misstatement risk, thereby reducing the need for greater auditor effort. Du et al. (2020) showed that socially responsible firms prefer selecting a Big 4 auditor and are less likely to switch, and that CSR activities are inversely related to audit engagement risk, leading to lower audit fees. However, Hekmat et al. (2023) found that social responsibility disclosures can increase audit report lag and effort, possibly due to the complexity of verifying such information. Given these conflicting findings, we formulate the second research hypothesis as follows: H2. The association between climate change risk related disclosures and audit efforts is affected by client ESG performance. 3.4 The impact of political connections on the relationship between climate risk related disclosures and audit efforts The influence of political connections on corporate behavior has long been a subject of scholarly interest (Faccio, 2006), particularly in emerging economies where such ties are widespread due to inefficient capital markets, weak legal enforcement, 218 and limited governmental oversight (Qi et al., 2023). Politically connected firms often enjoy preferential access to financing (Lashitew, 2014; Sohail et al., 2022), improved operational performance (Boubakri et al., 2012), and enhanced firm value (Wirawan et al., 2020). Recent studies (Qian & Chen, 2021; Luo et al., 2022; Mukhtaruddin et al., 2024) suggest that these firms are also more inclined to disclose information related to climate change and environmental issues, indicating a potential interaction between political ties and climate-related disclosures. Qian and Chen (2021), analyzing highly polluting Chinese firms in 2012 and 2015, found a positive association between the political connections of corporate chairpersons and environmental disclosure levels in 2015, but not in 2012. Luo et al. (2022) demonstrated that political connections moderate the relationship between legitimacy pressure and the quality and scope of carbon information disclosure. Specifically, the positive influence of legitimacy pressure on disclosure practices is more pronounced in politically connected firms. Supporting legitimacy theory, Mukhtaruddin et al. (2024) found that political connections positively affect sustainability disclosures among manufacturing firms listed on the Indonesian stock exchange, suggesting that such disclosures may be strategically used to facilitate access to external financing. Further empirical evidence highlights the impact of political connections on audit efforts (Aswadi et al., 2011; Hu et al., 2017; WahabSalehi, 2020; Ahmed et al., 2022). Aswadi et al. (2011) and WahabSalehi (2020) reported that politically connected firms tend to engage in more intensive audit processes and incur abnormal audit fees. Hu et al. (2017) found a positive association between a CEO’s political connections and the likelihood of receiving a favorable audit opinion in the subsequent period. Similarly, Ahmed et al. (2022) concluded that politically connected firms pay higher audit fees and require greater audit effort than their non-connected counterparts, largely due to the uncertainty and risk introduced by these affiliations. Based on this body of literature, we formulate the third research hypothesis as follows: H3: The association between climate change risk related disclosures and audit efforts is affected by client political connections. 4. Conclusion and implications This study provides comprehensive data from 2017 to 2022 to conduct an in-depth empirical investigation into how climate change risk related disclosures affect audit efforts. The results reveal that climate change related disclosures significantly necessitate higher audit efforts. The firm’s ESG practices and political connections significantly moderate the relationship between climate change disclosures and audit efforts, where the association between climates related disclosures and audit efforts is stronger when the firm has more EFG activities and political connections. Robustness tests confirmed our results using alternative measures for climate change disclosure, furthermore the results unchanged when Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) method was employed. Given the study`s findings and the growing interest in climate-related threats, several practical recommendations can be made for regulators, firm management, directors, auditors, and investors. First, regulators should work to develop a strategy to deal with climate change threats and enhance awareness about climate change including the usefulness of its related disclosure. Additionally, governmental agencies should set incentives for encouraging firms to develop mitigating mechanisms against climate change risks. Second, Managers and directors should improve climate change risk management mechanisms and enhance the transparency of climate-related disclosures. Third, auditors, it is becoming increasingly important to identify and consider climate-related risks while assessing client risks, planning audit procedures, and managing their client portfolio to support the sustainability of the business community against the climate change risks, furthermore auditors should focus on the effect on audit efforts and opinion about financial statements in case of disagreement between financial statements and other information included in annual report including climate change disclosures. Finally, investors should consider the impact of climate change disclosures on information asymmetry and gain an understanding about the possible inconsistencies between financial statements and other information related to climate risk exposure included in the company`s annual report. This study has a limitation related to the Egyptian professional environment and lack of information about the assigned number of hours by the responsible audit partner or the selected audit firm to make the audit and form the audit opinion, accordingly we have used the level of paid audit fees as a proxy for the level of devoted audit efforts. Future studies should investigate several related research areas including the impact of climate risk related disclosures on the borrowing cost, the mediating effect of information asymmetry on the relationship between climate change related disclosures and auditor`s litigation risk, and the moderating effect of auditor reputation on the relationship between climate risks related disclosures and financial reporting quality. JSON: Name: ccd_audit_effort_esg_pc_egypt Title: Panel regression and system-GMM analysis of how climate-change risk disclosures influence audit effort and how ESG performance and political connections moderate that relationship in Egyptian listed nonfinancial firms Short Hypothesis: Greater firm-level climate-change risk disclosure causes auditors to increase audit effort, and this causal effect is larger for firms with higher ESG performance or with political connections. Related Work: Existing empirical work has primarily used cross-sectional and panel regression methods to relate environmental disclosures or measured carbon exposure to audit fees or hours, with some studies applying text-analytics to quantify disclosure quality and others using index-based disclosure scores. Prior studies differ on modeling choices (pooled OLS, firm fixed effects, or clustered standard errors) and on endogeneity handling (limited use of instrumental or dynamic-panel estimators). Research that examines moderators typically focuses on single dimensions (e.g., auditor size or corporate governance) rather than jointly testing ESG performance and political ties. Limitations include: inconsistent measurement of climate disclosures (binary, index, or text-derived measures), reliance on audit fees as an imperfect proxy for audit effort, limited attention to reverse causality and omitted variable bias, sparse use of dynamic-panel approaches for persistent outcomes, and a paucity of studies in emerging markets where political connections are prevalent. These gaps leave unresolved whether observed associations reflect causal auditor responses and how ESG and political ties condition that response. Abstract: This study investigates whether firm-level climate-change risk disclosures causally increase auditor effort and whether Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) performance and political connections amplify that effect. Using a panel of Egyptian nonfinancial listed firms from 2017–2022, we estimate firm-year panel regressions with industry and year fixed effects and apply system generalized method of moments (GMM) to address simultaneity and persistence. Climate-change disclosure is operationalized with a TCFD-based item score and an alternative median-split binary indicator; audit effort is proxied by the natural log of audit fees. We estimate interaction models to test moderation by ESG ratings and a board-level political-connection indicator. Main contributions are: (1) identifying a positive causal effect of disclosure on audit effort in an emerging market sample, (2) demonstrating that the disclosure–effort link is stronger for higher-ESG and politically connected firms, and (3) triangulating results with robustness tests including alternative disclosure measures, subsample analyses, and dynamic-panel estimators. Expected outcomes inform how auditors price climate-related business risk and how firm characteristics condition audit resource allocation. Experiments: Datasets: Firm-level panel of Egyptian Exchange (EGX) top firms, nonfinancial firms, annual observations 2017–2022; sources: annual reports, Mubasher Egypt, Bloomberg Asharq, EGX disclosure datasets, S&P/EGX ESG ratings; sample: ~80 firms, ~480 firm-year observations. Variables: Dependent = ln(audit_fees); Primary independent = continuous TCFD-based climate disclosure score (0–1) and binary CCD_median (1 if above sample median); Moderators = continuous ESG_score (annual S&P/EGX rating normalized) and PC_dummy (1 if board contains political actors/relatives). Controls = firm_size_ln, roa, leverage, board_size, big4_dummy, loss_dummy, industry FE, year FE. Baselines: (A) pooled OLS with robust SE; (B) firm fixed-effects (FE); (C) FE with clustered SE by firm-year; (D) dynamic-panel system GMM (two-step) with lagged dependent as instrument. Estimation and tests: Hausman test to choose FE vs RE; VIF for multicollinearity; White-robust SE; AR(1)/AR(2) and Hansen J for GMM validity. Evaluation metrics: coefficient estimates and t-stats for CCD, interaction terms, adjusted R2, change in predicted audit fees for 1-SD CCD increase, p-values for robustness tests. Comparisons/Ablations: 1) Compare models A–D to assess estimator sensitivity. 2) Ablation 1: drop ESG interaction to test marginal effect of CCD*PC alone. 3) Ablation 2: drop PC interaction to test CCD*ESG alone. 4) Alternative CCD measures: text-derived disclosure clarity score and median-split binary. 5) Subsample tests: Big4 vs non-Big4 auditors; high vs low litigation industries; pre- vs post-regulation (pre-2022 vs 2022). 6) Placebo test: regress future audit fees on current CCD lag to assess reverse causality. Reporting: tabulate main coefficients, interaction marginal effects, robustness columns, GMM diagnostics, and subsample coefficient heterogeneity. Risk Factors and Limitations: Measurement error: TCFD-based disclosure scoring and ESG ratings may contain subjectivity and reporting heterogeneity; political-connection coding may misclassify informal ties. Proxy validity: audit fees imperfectly reflect audit effort due to fee negotiations, client bargaining power, or non-audit service mixes. Endogeneity: reverse causality and omitted variables (unobserved risk factors, managerial quality) may bias estimates; system GMM may face weak instruments or instrument proliferation. Sample size and external validity: modest sample (≈480 observations) reduces statistical power for high-dimensional interactions and limits generalization beyond Egyptian nonfinancial listed firms. Time window: regulatory changes during the sample (mandates effective 2022) create structural breaks and limit pre-policy variation. Heterogeneity and scalability: results may not extend to countries with different audit markets or political economies. Estimation risks: multicollinearity between CCD, ESG, and firm size may inflate SEs; heteroskedasticity and serial correlation require careful inference. Data availability: absence of direct audit-hours or partner-level effort measures prevents validation of fee-based inferences.
